processes.description: A round starts when someone in risk, credit, settlements or the trading desk spots a deal booked wrong: the wrong counterparty, a missing EOL or Sitara link, a physical deal not marked for its financial component, or double entry. Darron Giron or Bill Williams asks the booker to change the counterparty in Tagg, update the link fields or rebook the deal, and confirms once the deal looks right in both Tagg and Sitara. Some rounds become a larger reconciliation against another party's records before deals can be valued.
steps: Someone notices a booking problem, from credit, a DPR or SAR run, or a counterparty query.
The deal is looked up in Tagg, Sitara or Enpower and compared with what was traded.
The correct counterparty short name, deal type or link number is identified.
The booker is asked to rebook, relink or change the counterparty.
The deal is changed, or zeroed out and re-entered when it was a duplicate.
The requester checks both systems and confirms the deal is booked correctly.

stalls.summary: A booker could not change the counterparty in the system and had to ask someone else to make the correction.
A transport deal correction was passed along to another person and then needed a follow-up asking whether anyone had looked at it yet.
Deals that could not be reconciled against another party's records had to be started over and rebooked from scratch.
Double deal entry in a book had to be found from the DPR and SAR and zeroed out the next morning.

contradictions.summary: One note praises a dramatic improvement in the accuracy of deal entry in Enpower, while within days another reports double deal entry that had to be zeroed out.

automation.approach: A nightly exception report comparing Tagg, Sitara and Enpower could flag deals with missing EOL or Sitara links, counterparty names that do not match the credit-approved short name, physical deals without the financial flag, and duplicate entries in the same book, so bookers receive a list of specific fixes instead of one-off emails.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same few checks (counterparty short name, link fields, deal classification, duplicates). A booking checklist used at entry time would catch them before credit or settlements does, and is something the desk can adopt immediately before any report is built.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds involve looking up one or a few deals in Tagg and Sitara, finding the right counterparty or link number and rebooking, around 20 minutes. The high end covers rounds like reconciling a set of deals against another party or zeroing out duplicate entries. Detection and cross-system matching suit a report; the rebooking decision stays with people.

processes.description: When a business is sold or handed over (HPL to AEP, then the North American gas and power trading business to UBS), staff circulate transition memos, lists of files and directories, rosters of traders, profit centers and procedures, and data copying protocols. Owners ask others to review memos and send changes, list which procedures the estate team must keep running, enter test deals after system cutovers, and copy compliant data to the new environment by a stated deadline such as midnight CST, Thursday, February 7, 2002.
steps: A coordinator circulates a memo or plan of transition issues and asks for review.
Desks list the files, directories, procedures and traders that move or stay.
Rosters, profit centers and status files for the new owner are compiled and sent.
Systems are separated and test deals are entered after databases come back up.
Staff copy permitted data and documents to the new environment by the deadline.
Remaining duties such as daily settlements are assigned to the estate team.

stalls.summary: A desk head contacted several people for direction on their transition status and was still waiting for a response.

automation.approach: A shared transition tracker listing each file share, procedure, system and person with its destination (new owner or estate), status and owner would replace the repeated memos and roster requests, with a standard data-migration checklist for each desk.
automation.rationale: The rounds keep rebuilding the same lists of people, procedures, files and profit centers. One tracker layout gathers them once, makes review easier and shows what is still open.

work_estimate.rationale: Rounds involve compiling a roster or file list, reviewing and updating a transition memo, entering test deals or copying documents to the new environment. Each of those is roughly 45 minutes of hands-on work; memo drafting and data copying sit at the high end. Much of it is judgement about what moves, so only the list keeping suits a tool.

processes.description: A coordinator asks the team to submit their planned vacation for the coming month, or a staff member confirms their own days. People announce when they will be out and list who covers each of their duties, such as error reports or sending nominations, or name one colleague to handle the whole desk. A manager approves short-notice time off and asks that longer vacations be raised in advance.
steps: The coordinator asks staff to submit the coming month's vacation dates.
Staff send or confirm their vacation days.
The manager approves the time off.
The absent person announces the dates and names who covers each duty.

automation.approach: A shared team calendar with a time-off request form that captures dates and a coverage assignment for each duty, sending the approval and the coverage announcement from the same entry.
automation.rationale: Each round gathers the same fields: dates, approval, and who covers which task. A form with a coverage table makes sure every duty has a named cover and saves rebuilding the list each time.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work beyond the emails is checking dates against the team schedule, recording them and arranging cover for each duty, around 5 minutes per round. A calendar and request form could do the recording and conflict checks.
